info.text: Unit 12 — Simulation: avionics fault-find. Listening, reading, use of English and vocabulary at CEFR B2.

name.text: L1 · Dialogue 1 — what the fault code points to

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. When the BITE returns the fault code, what does the lead technician say it points towards?

generalfeedback.text: The lead says the code "points towards the data bus, rather than the display screen itself". That is why they trace the wiring before condemning the expensive box.

feedback.text: Correct — the code points to the data bus, so they trace the wiring first.
No — the lead says the fault is not the screen, which may be serviceable.
No — the pilot report is accepted; the code points to the data bus.
No — the battery is never mentioned; the code points to the data bus.

name.text: L2 · Dialogue 1 — order of work

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. The technicians decide to replace the display box first, and only trace the wiring afterwards.

generalfeedback.text: False. Because a replacement box is expensive, they trace the wiring first. The box is swapped only if the wiring is proved good.

feedback.text: No — they trace the wiring first, because the box is expensive.
Correct — wiring is traced first; the box is a last resort.

name.text: L3 · Dialogue 2 — why disconnect first

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. Why must the connector be disconnected before the continuity check?

generalfeedback.text: The lead warns: "you must never test a live circuit". A continuity check is done on a dead circuit, so the connector is opened first.

answer.text: So the circuit is not live

feedback.text: Correct — you must never test a live circuit for continuity.

answer.text: Because the multimeter needs charging first

feedback.text: No — this is a safety point about live circuits, not the meter's battery.

answer.text: So the fault code can be cleared quickly

feedback.text: No — clearing the code is not the reason to disconnect.

answer.text: Because pin five must be removed first

feedback.text: No — no pin is removed; the whole connector is opened for safety.

name.text: L4 · Dialogue 2 — pin five reading

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. Pin five was found to be healthy, with a resistance close to zero.

generalfeedback.text: True. Pin five reads almost zero ohms, which shows a whole, unbroken conductor. Only pin four was open.

feedback.text: Correct — pin five reads near zero, so that conductor is good.
No — pin five was the healthy one; pin four was open.

name.text: L5 · Dialogue 1 — number of fault codes

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. How many separate fault codes did the BITE return? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: One. The BITE "returned a single fault code" — 27-FC-114. A clean, single code makes the fault easier to trace.

feedback.text: Correct — a single fault code was returned.

name.text: L6 · Dialogue 1 — number of data pins

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 1 again. How many pins carry the display data through the connector? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: Two. The diagram shows the data travelling on pin four and pin five, through connector D-27A.

feedback.text: Correct — pin four and pin five, so two pins.

name.text: L7 · Dialogue 2 — the open pin

questiontext.text: Listen to Dialogue 2 again. On which pin number was the open circuit found? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: Pin four. It showed an extremely high value with no path — a classic open circuit. Pin five was healthy.

feedback.text: Correct — the open circuit was on pin four.

name.text: L8 · Dialogue 4 — tests before flight

questiontext.text: Listen to the shift-handover message (Dialogue 4) again. How many functional tests are still required before the first flight? Write the number.

generalfeedback.text: One. Nadia asks the morning team to "carry out one more functional test before the first flight". Everything else is complete.

feedback.text: Correct — one more functional test is required.

name.text: R1 · Service Bulletin — the cause

questiontext.text:
Read this Service Bulletin, then answer.

SERVICE BULLETIN 34-1187 (category: recommended). Some nav display units show a blank screen after long flights. The cause is a chafed data wire near connector D-27A, where the harness passes a metal bracket. This bulletin adds a protective sleeve over the harness at that point. The work takes about one hour. It is optional, but operators with two or more blank-screen events should carry it out at the next check.

According to the bulletin, what causes the blank screen?

generalfeedback.text: The bulletin names "a chafed data wire near connector D-27A", worn where the harness rubs a metal bracket. The fix protects that spot with a sleeve.

feedback.text: Correct — the wire is chafed where it passes a metal bracket.
No — the display unit board is not blamed; the wire is chafed.

answer.text: A software error in the BITE

feedback.text: No — the bulletin describes a wiring problem, not software.

answer.text: A loose bracket in the cockpit

feedback.text: No — the bracket is the rubbing point, but the fault is the chafed wire.

name.text: R2 · Service Bulletin — is it mandatory?

questiontext.text: Read Service Bulletin 34-1187 again (see question R1). The bulletin is mandatory for all operators.

generalfeedback.text: False. The bulletin is "category: recommended" and "optional". Only operators with two or more events are advised to do it. A mandatory instruction would be an Airworthiness Directive (AD).

feedback.text: No — it is recommended and optional, not mandatory.
Correct — it is recommended/optional; an AD would be mandatory.

name.text: R3 · Service Bulletin — the fix

questiontext.text: Read Service Bulletin 34-1187 again (see question R1). What does the bulletin add to protect the harness?

generalfeedback.text: It "adds a protective sleeve over the harness" at the point where it passes the bracket, so the wire can no longer chafe.

feedback.text: Correct — a sleeve is added over the harness at the bracket.
No — no extra connector is fitted; a sleeve is added.
No — the bracket is the cause of the chafe, not the fix.
No — bonding is not the issue here; a protective sleeve is added.

name.text: R4 · Work Order — release decision

questiontext.text:
Read this Work Order, then answer.

WORK ORDER WO-55821. Task: functional test of the number-one nav display after a harness repair. Steps: apply power, run the BITE, and confirm a clean pass with no fault code. Then check the display in day and night brightness. Record the result in the tech log. If any fault code returns, do not release the aircraft; raise a new work order and inform the duty engineer.

If a fault code returns during the test, the technician may still release the aircraft.

generalfeedback.text: False. The work order is explicit: "If any fault code returns, do not release the aircraft." A new work order is raised and the duty engineer is informed.

feedback.text: No — a returning fault code means the aircraft must not be released.
Correct — do not release; raise a new work order instead.

name.text: R5 · Work Order — what to confirm

questiontext.text: Read Work Order WO-55821 again (see question R4). What must the technician confirm when the BITE is run?

generalfeedback.text: The order says "confirm a clean pass with no fault code". Only then may the brightness checks and the release proceed.

feedback.text: Correct — a clean pass with no fault code is required.
No — any returning fault code stops the release.
No — the BITE step confirms a clean pass, not a connector number.
No — a high reading means an open circuit; the BITE must pass cleanly.

name.text: U1 · Sequencing — first step

questiontext.text:
Add ONE sequencing word for the very first action. Use a capital letter.

"____, run the BITE self-test."

generalfeedback.text: First (or To start) marks step one. Do not use At first, which means "in the beginning, but it changed later".

feedback.text: Correct — First marks step one.
Also correct — To start marks step one.
Use First (or To start) for step one, not At first.

name.text: U2 · Sequencing — last step

questiontext.text:
Add ONE sequencing word for the last action. Use a capital letter.

"____, sign the tech log and hand the aircraft back."

generalfeedback.text: Finally (or Lastly / In the end) marks the last step of a procedure.

feedback.text: Correct — Finally marks the last step.
Also correct — Lastly marks the last step.
Also correct — In the end marks the last step.
Use Finally, Lastly or In the end for the last step.

name.text: U3 · Article before a known thing

questiontext.text:
Add the ONE missing word.

"Next, measure ____ pin voltage at the box."

generalfeedback.text: English needs the before a thing that is already known. Latvian and Russian have no articles, so this word is easy to drop.

feedback.text: Correct — the pin voltage (a known, specific thing).
The missing word is the.

name.text: U4 · Modal + base verb

questiontext.text: One extra word is wrong in this sentence: "First you must to open the connector." Write the ONE word that must be removed.

generalfeedback.text: After a modal such as must, can, should, use the base verb alone: must open, not must to open. Remove to.

feedback.text: Correct — remove to: "you must open the connector".
Remove to — a modal is followed by the base verb.

name.text: U5 · Term gap — no current path

questiontext.text:
Fill the gap with a term from the unit (two words).

"A break in the conductor, where no current can flow, is an ____ ____."

generalfeedback.text: An open circuit is a break where the path is interrupted, so a meter reads a very high value with no path.

feedback.text: Correct — an open circuit.
The term is open circuit.

name.text: U6 · Term gap — the meter test

questiontext.text:
Fill the gap with a term from the unit (two words).

"The meter test that confirms a wire is whole from end to end is a ____ ____."

generalfeedback.text: A continuity check confirms that a conductor is unbroken. You do or run a continuity check.

feedback.text: Correct — a continuity check.
The term is continuity check.

name.text: U7 · Term gap — live wire to airframe

questiontext.text:
Fill the gap with a term from the unit (two words).

"A fault where a live conductor touches the metal airframe is a ____ ____."

generalfeedback.text: A ground fault is a live conductor touching the airframe, which it should never do. Check for it after finding an open circuit.

feedback.text: Correct — a ground fault.
The term is ground fault.

name.text: U8 · Time conjunction for a waiting step

questiontext.text:
Join the two steps with ONE time word (a step that waits for another). Use a capital letter.

"____ you find the break, open the tape carefully."

generalfeedback.text: Once, As soon as, When or After all mark a step that waits for the one before it.

feedback.text: Correct — Once marks a waiting step.
Also correct — As soon as marks a waiting step.
Also correct — When marks a waiting step.
Also correct — After marks a waiting step.
Use Once, As soon as, When or After.

name.text: V1 · Match the term to its meaning

questiontext.text: Match each avionics term to its plain meaning.

generalfeedback.text: BITE tests itself; a fault code names the fault; the WDM is the wiring book; an LRU is a swappable box; a harness is a wire bundle; a splice is a joint between two conductors.

answer.text: a number that names the fault
a box you can swap on the line
a joint where two wires are joined

name.text: V2 · Match the term to its verb (collocation)

questiontext.text: Match each term to the verb that goes with it in the workshop.

generalfeedback.text: You run the BITE, read a fault code, disconnect a connector, probe a pin, do a continuity check, and set the multimeter.

name.text: V3 · Which word means a wire bundle?

questiontext.text: Which term means "a bundle of wires taped together and routed as one assembly"?

generalfeedback.text: A harness is the taped bundle of wires. A connector joins harnesses; a terminal is an end fitting; a multimeter is the test tool.

feedback.text: Correct — the harness is the taped bundle of wires.
No — a connector is the plug that joins two harnesses.
No — a terminal is the end fitting of a single conductor.
No — a multimeter is the meter you test with.

name.text: V4 · Complete the collocation

questiontext.text:
Choose the correct verb to complete the collocation:

"Before you probe, ____ the multimeter to continuity."

generalfeedback.text: We set the multimeter to a range or function. "Make", "open" and "read" do not collocate with a meter's setting.

feedback.text: Correct — set the multimeter to continuity.
No — we do not "make" a meter to a range; we set it.
No — you open a connector, but you set a meter.
No — you read the value after you set the meter.
